rv.q: This thought-provoking anthology brings together five playwrights to reflect upon the causes, complexities and human cost of the war.
Ukraine Unbroken packs a punch, rising in both power and horror over the course of the evening.
This agonising splinter of a play drives to the heart of what it might feel like first to lose a child and then to recover them, fundamentally altered.
They are uneven but, together, they are so worthwhile.
There is a sense of a group of artists coming together in the belief that something must be said; that theatre cannot apathetically sit back; that uncomfortable truths and hideous memories matter.
And great charm is woven between scenes by Mariia Petrovksa crooning and plucking a bandura - a zither-lute hybrid which is the national instrument of Ukraine.
It ends on a high with Cat Goscovitch’s Taken, which depicts a mother trying to get back her 12-year-old daughter, who has been abducted by the Russians.
Ukraine Unbroken is determined to meet the challenge of archiving in real time, and does so with conviction and urgency.
Ukraine Unbroken is a well-structured, emotionally powerful night at the theatre.
By the third playlet – the best of the five – Three Mates by Natalka Vorozhbit, we are 1,468 days into the war, and the enemy is no longer just the one outside dropping bombs on civilians.
The individual plays vary in style and content but give an intriguing and strong presentation of the situation for Ukraine and its people.

Although it was never difficult to follow proceedings, they were sometimes bogged down in details, to the point where parts of the show felt more like information dissemination than theatrical performance.
Unfortunately, however, the pieces are too uneven to add up to a satisfying evening of theatre.
So that’s it: Ukraine Unbroken, an extraordinary evening.
On the whole, an excellent piece of theatre.

cn.t: Five uneven but worthwhile plays trace Ukraine's recent history with compassion and power, though the evening runs long. Critics praise the focus on ordinary people caught in war and strong performances, particularly musician Mariia Petrovska.
